passages.title: The first revelation: read by your Lord's name
passages.tafsir:
These are the first words of the Qur'an ever revealed — the moment prophethood began, in a cave above Makkah, with a command to a man who could not read. The five ayat name the Lord who created (ayah 1), who created man from a clinging clot (ayah 2), who is the Most Generous (ayah 3), who taught by the pen (ayah 4), and who taught man what he did not know (ayah 5). Ibn Kathir says of them that they are "the first mercy that Allah bestowed upon His servants and the first bounty that Allah favored them with."

## The night it began

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that it is universally agreed — citing Baghawi, and noting that Bukhari, Muslim, other authentic sources and the overwhelming consensus of scholars ancient and modern all concur — that these five verses mark the very beginning of Qur'anic revelation. Both commentaries build on the long narration of Sayyidah ʿA'ishah: Ibn Kathir notes that Imam Ahmad recorded it and that it is in the Two Sahihs by way of Az-Zuhri; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites it from the Sahihs of Bukhari and Muslim.

**It began with dreams.** The first thing that came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from the revelation was true dreams in his sleep — he would not see a dream except that it came true as clearly as the break of dawn. Then seclusion became beloved to him. He would withdraw to the cave of Hira' and devote himself to worship there for a number of nights, taking provisions, then return to Khadijah and replenish them for a similar stretch. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the cave lies in the mountain known today as Jabal an-Nur, visible in front of Jannat al-Maʿla, the famous graveyard of Makkah, and that reports differ on the length of his stay — the report of the Sahihain putting it at a month, the whole month of Ramadan.

**What was he doing in there?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is honest: the authentic traditions are silent about the mode of worship he adopted. Some scholars suggested he worshipped according to the law of Nuh, Ibrahim or ʿIsa (peace be upon them), but it rejects this — no authentic report supports it, and it is unlikely, since he was *ummiyy*, unlettered. More likely his worship was concentration and reflection upon Allah Almighty and His omnipotence.

**Then the angel came.** "Read!" And he answered, *mā anā bi-qāri'* — "I am not one who reads." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the reply: he was under the impression that the angel was directing him to read a written document, and since he could neither read nor write, he answered accordingly. The angel seized him and pressed him until he could bear no more, released him, and said "Read!" The same answer. A second pressing. The same answer. A third — and then these five ayat, from *Read in the Name of your Lord who created* through to *that which he knew not*.

**He came home shaking.** He returned with those ayat, his heart trembling, until he came to Khadijah, saying *zammilūnī zammilūnī* — "Wrap me up, wrap me up!" They wrapped him until the awe left him. Then he told her everything that had happened and said, "I fear for myself." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains this fear: it was due to the great responsibility delegated to him, and due to the unusual event of seeing an angel in his original form.

Khadijah's reply is an argument from character: "Never! By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You keep good relations with your relatives, you speak the truth, you help the poor and the destitute, you serve your guests generously, and you help the deserving, calamity-afflicted people." She did not tell him to calm down. She told him what he was, and reasoned that Allah does not disgrace such a man.

**Waraqah.** She took him to her cousin Waraqah bin Nawfal — an old man who had lost his eyesight, who had become a Christian during the days of ignorance (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes this was a true religion at that time) and who used to write the Scriptures in Arabic, writing from the Injil in Hebrew as much as Allah willed. He heard the account and said: "This is *An-Nāmūs*" — the confidant, the angel Jibril (peace be upon him) — "whom Allah sent to Musa. I wish I were young; I wish I were alive when your people expel you." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked in surprise, "Will they drive me out?" Waraqah replied yes: anyone who came with something similar to what you have brought was met with hostility and enmity — and if I should remain alive till that day, I would firmly support you.

Waraqah did not remain. He died, and the revelation paused. Ibn Kathir relates what followed, flagging it himself with the words "according to what we were told": the Messenger of Allah ﷺ became sad, and out of that grief he set out a number of times with the intent of throwing himself from the mountain tops. But every time he reached the peak of a mountain to throw himself from it, Jibril would appear to him and say, "O Muhammad! You are truly the Messenger of Allah!" — at which his worry would be eased, his soul would be settled, and he would return down from the mountain. Then, when the revelation did not come again for a long time, he set out as he had done before, and again Jibril appeared and said to him the same as he had said before. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazhari, records that the break lasted about a year and a half according to Suhaili, while other reports say about three years.

**Read these five on their own.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that only these five ayat belong to that first night; ayat 6–19 are of much later date, revealed in connection with an incident in which Abu Jahl prevented the Prophet ﷺ from offering salah. In the initial stages of revelation and prophethood he had no enemies in Makkah — all used to call him *al-Amīn*, the honest and upright — and they respected and loved him. Abu Jahl's enmity clearly began only once the Prophet ﷺ proclaimed his call publicly and prayed in the Sacred Mosque; and salah was prescribed on the Night of Ascent (Miʿraj), so being prevented from it cannot be imagined before that time.

**Which surah came first?** Some scholars held Sūrah al-Muddaththir was revealed first, others Sūrah al-Fatihah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reconciles the views, citing Mazhari: after Sūrah al-ʿAlaq there was the temporary break, during which the Prophet ﷺ used to be very sad; then Jibril appeared to him once more and the opening verses of al-Muddaththir were conveyed — so al-Muddaththir was the first surah revealed *after the break*. And the Companions who named al-Fatihah probably meant that it was the first surah revealed in *complete* form, all seven ayat at once — whereas from al-ʿAlaq, al-Muzzammil and al-Muddaththir only some verses came first, the rest at later dates.

## The words themselves

**"In the Name of your Lord" (ayah 1).** Why *bismi rabbika* and not simply "Read"? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazhari, finds the addition of *ismi* significant in two ways. First, that whenever the Qur'an is recited, the reader should begin with *Bismillāhir-Raḥmānir-Raḥīm*. Second — the tender one — the man had just apologised that he was unable to read, being unlettered. The phrase points to the fact that under present circumstances you may be *ummiyy*, but Allah has the power to grant you the highest level of knowledge and the most elegant eloquence, so that you would surpass and subdue the most educated among people — as indeed became manifest later on.

**Why the name *Rabb*?** Allah has many Beautiful Names; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān suggests *Rabb* is chosen here probably because it supports the theme that Allah cherishes and sustains the Prophet ﷺ through all the different stages of his development until he is fully consummated. That Lord can make him read and recite despite his being unlettered.

**"Who created" — created *what*?** A grammatical detail with enormous reach. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that *khalaqa* is a transitive verb — it requires an object — and the object is absent here. That absence indicates the verb is used absolutely: the Creator has created the entire universe and every existent thing it contains. Why lead with the attribute of creating? Because the first divine favour is *wujūd*, existence itself — His drawing beings out of the realm of non-existence into the realm of existence. Many other favours of His follow.

**From the whole to the one (ayah 2).** Ayah 1 referred to the creation of the macrocosm, the entire universe in general; ayah 2 narrows to the microcosm — man, whom Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls the epitome of the macrocosm, a small-scale representation or miniature of the large and complex universe. Man is mentioned particularly because the purpose of prophethood, messengerhood and the revelation of the Qur'an is that divine injunctions be implemented and acted upon — and that is mankind's essential peculiarity.

***ʿAlaq.*** The word is the plural of *ʿalaqah*, congealed blood — Ibn Kathir renders it "a dangling clot." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets it in sequence: man's primordial creation is from the four major elements — earth, water, fire and air; his procreation is from an insignificant and humble state, the sperm, which then transforms into congealed blood, the primary state of the embryo after conception, then takes the shape of a lump of flesh, and then the skeletal structure is created. *ʿAlaqah* is the middle phase, and mentioning it specifically covers the initial and final stages of the whole process.

**"Read!" a second time (ayah 3).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two reasons for the repetition. The first *iqra'* (ayah 1) was for the Prophet ﷺ himself to read and recite; the second is a command to proclaim, convey, communicate, teach and preach. And it is not inconceivable that the command is repeated by deliberate design for emphasis.

***Al-Akram*, the Most Generous.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this divine attribute signifies that Allah did not create the world or man for any ulterior motive, for selfish motivation, or for His own benefit. He did it out of His infinite grace, generosity and magnanimity: He endowed upon the universe the great favour of existence without its asking for it.

## The pen (ayah 4)

The preceding ayah spoke of the creation of man; ayah 4 speaks of his education — because knowledge, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, distinguishes man from all other animals and creatures and occupies the position of the crown of creation. There are two media through which knowledge is imparted: the oral or spoken, and the pen or written. The command *iqra'* at the surah's opening refers to the oral; this ayah speaks of the written method of recording and transmitting knowledge from generation to generation.

**On the divine Pen.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates an authentic narration of Sayyidna Abu Hurairah that the Messenger of Allah said: "When Allah created the creation, He inscribed a document which is with Him above the Throne: Indeed My mercy has preceded My anger." It also relates, citing Qurtubi, another narration in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The first thing Allah created was the pen. He told it to write, so it wrote what was to take place till Doomsday. This is with Allah on His Throne." (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names no hadith collection for either narration.)

**Three kinds of pen.** Scholars, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān citing Qurtubi, speak of three pens in the world: a Pen that Allah created with His own hand and instructed to write the decree of the universe; the pen of the angels, who record the events that are to occur and their magnitude, and with it record the deeds of human beings; and the pen of human beings, which they use to reduce their speech to writing — writing being, in fact, a kind of speech, and speech a faculty for which Allah has programmed man, natural and innate. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then reports that Mujahid — whom it calls the leading authority on Tafsir — cites from Abu ʿAmr that Allah created four things in the entire universe with His own Creative hand, the rest of creation coming into being by His cosmic command *kun*, "be": the pen, the Divine Throne, the Garden of Eden, and Adam (peace be upon him).

**What the pen is worth.** Sayyidna Qatadah stated that the pen is a great divine gift: had Allah not granted man this art, it would not have been possible to preserve the religion in its pristine form, nor to conduct worldly affairs properly. Sayyidna ʿAli stated that it is a great generosity that Allah granted His servants knowledge of things they did not know, drawing them out of the darkness of ignorance into the light of knowledge — and he urged people to acquire the skill, for its benefits are great. Only Allah is able to keep count of them: sciences and philosophies codified, the histories and chronicles of former and later nations compiled and preserved, and the divinely revealed Books committed to writing, to be preserved as long as the world lasts. Without the pen, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, all worldly and religious works would come to a standstill. It also laments that in this age students and scholars have ignored the importance of this art — "To Allah do we direct our complaint!"

## The real Teacher (ayah 5)

Ayah 4 was concerned with one particular means of teaching, the pen. Ayah 5 mentions no means at all — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads that silence as the point: the real teacher is Allah, and He has innumerable ways and means, besides the pen, of imparting knowledge.

Man is taught from the very inception of his life. First he is gifted with intellect, the greatest means of receiving knowledge, by whose right use he understands many things. Further, his entire environment is a manifestation of the perfect power of Allah, studded with evidence of divine power, by witnessing which he can recognise his Creator. Revelation and inspiration are other means. And many essential things are learnt intuitively — intuition being the ability, given by Allah, to know or understand through feeling rather than by weighing facts, so that neither tongue nor pen is needed. When a baby is born it knows nothing of how its environment works, yet it instinctively reaches for its mother when hungry; and Allah has taught it the "skill" of crying from birth, so that its cry becomes the means of satisfying hunger, thirst, heat and cold, and a cause of concern for its parents to find out what is wrong. Who teaches the newborn to cry? After this instinctive knowledge, man's knowledge continues to increase by word of mouth, and then by the supra-rational organ of intuition, called the heart.

**Why say "what he did not know"?** Apparently there was no need for the phrase, since knowledge is normally imparted of things not known. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazhari, explains that it is stated explicitly probably so that man may not assume that the knowledge and skills Allah gave him are the results of his own efforts and exertion. It is added to make man realise that there was a time when he knew nothing — as in 16:78, *And Allah has brought you forth from your mothers' wombs when you knew nothing*. This shows that knowledge is not an ingrained personal excellence of man; it is the gift of the Creator and Master.

## What Ibn Kathir draws from all five

Ibn Kathir's summary is the passage's heart: the first thing revealed of the Qur'an were these noble and blessed ayat, and they are "the first mercy that Allah bestowed upon His servants and the first bounty that Allah favored them with." He states the principle plainly under the heading that the honour and nobility of man lie in his knowledge: these ayat inform of the beginning of man's creation from a dangling clot, and that out of Allah's generosity He taught man what he did not know — and thus Allah exalted him and honoured him by giving him knowledge, the dignity by which the father of humanity, Adam, was distinguished over the angels.

He also gives a neat anatomy of knowledge: it is sometimes in the mind, sometimes on the tongue, and sometimes in writing with the fingers — intellectual, spoken and written — and while the written necessitates the first two, the reverse is not true. For this reason, he says, Allah says *Read! And your Lord is the Most Generous. Who has taught by the pen. He has taught man that which he knew not.* He closes with a narration that states, "Record knowledge by writing," and a saying which states, "Whoever acts according to what he knows, Allah will make him inherit knowledge that he did not know."

## Living it

**Start where he started.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from *bismi rabbika* that whenever the Qur'an is recited, the reader should begin with *Bismillāhir-Raḥmānir-Raḥīm*. Reading is not a neutral act; it is done in a Name. And your inability is not the obstacle you take it for: he answered three times that he could not read, and was told to read — with a reminder of *whose* Name he was to read in, and with the assurance that Allah has the power to grant knowledge and eloquence to one who never learned letters.

**Write it down, and act on it.** Ibn Kathir cites a narration to record knowledge by writing; Qatadah calls the pen a great divine gift; ʿAli urged people to acquire the skill. And the saying Ibn Kathir cites makes learning a chain: whoever acts according to what he knows, Allah will make him inherit knowledge he did not know.

**Stay humble.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says ayah 5 is worded as it is so that man does not assume his knowledge and skills are the result of his own effort. There was a time when you knew nothing at all. Knowledge is not an ingrained personal excellence; it is the gift of the Creator and Master — and *al-Akram* gives without being asked.

passages.title: Man transgresses when he feels self-sufficient
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat diagnose a single spiritual disease and then administer its cure. Ayah 6 states the symptom — man overstepping every limit; ayah 7 names the cause — his imagining that he needs nobody; ayah 8 delivers the remedy — the reminder that everything is heading back to its Lord. Read together they form one argument: *you transgress because you think you are self-sufficient; you are not, and you are returning to the One who actually is.*

The surah opened with **"Read! In the Name of your Lord Who has created"** (ayah 1) — man addressed as a creature, made and taught by his Lord. Ayah 6 turns to what that same creature does when he forgets it.

---

## The moment behind the words

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that although the wording is general, the ayah "immediately refers to a particular person, namely, Abu Jahl who insulted the Holy Prophet ﷺ."

Ibn Kathir preserves a scene from that period. Ibn Jarir recorded from Abu Hurayrah — and Imam Ahmad bin Hanbal, Muslim, An-Nasaʾi and Ibn Abi Hatim all recorded this hadith — that Abu Jahl asked the people, "Does Muhammad cover his face with dust while he is among you all?" They replied, "Yes." Then he swore by Al-Lat and Al-ʿUzza that if he saw him praying like that, "I will stomp on his neck, and I will certainly put his face in the dust."

Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came and began to pray, "which made it possible for Abu Jahl to stomp on his neck." But the people were surprised at him, because he began retreating on his heels and covering himself with his hands. When he was asked what was the matter with him, he replied, "Verily, between me and him is a ditch of fire, monsters and wings." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then said, **"If he had come near me, the angels would have snatched him limb by limb."**

The narrator added a caution worth keeping in view: "Allah revealed an Ayah, but I do not know whether it is concerning the Hadith of Abu Hurayrah or not: *Nay! Verily, man does transgress* — to the end of the Surah." So the connection is reported, but the narrator himself did not claim certainty about it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the portrait of the man and states plainly why he belongs beside this ayah: Abu Jahl "was one of the well-to-do and prosperous people of Makkah. All the members of his tribe and inhabitants of the city respected and obeyed him. He became arrogant and insulted the leader of all the Prophets — the noblest of creation." He was, in the commentary's words, "a typical example of this."

---

## Ayah 6 — "Most certainly, one exceeds all bounds"

Look at how the three renderings before us handle the ayah. Ibn Kathir: "*Nay! Verily, man does transgress*." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: "*The fact is that man crosses the limits*." Our translation: "*Most certainly, one exceeds all bounds*." Whichever shade you take, the picture is the same — not merely doing wrong, but going past a boundary; a creature stepping outside the limits set for him.

Notice, too, who the subject is: **al-insān** — "man," the human being as such, not a named enemy. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that even though the immediate reference was Abu Jahl, "the statement is general which draws man's attention to one of his weaknesses." That is the difference between a verse of history and a verse of scripture. If ayah 6 had said "Abu Jahl transgresses," we could read it as someone else's obituary. It says *man*. You are included.

Ibn Kathir sums up the state being described: man is "very pleased, most evil, scornful and transgressive."

---

## Ayah 7 — "once they think they are self-sufficient"

This is the diagnostic ayah, and everything hinges on a single feature of its wording: it does not say man transgresses *because he is* self-sufficient. It says he transgresses once he **sees himself** as being so.

Look again at the renderings. Ibn Kathir: "when he **considers himself** self-sufficient." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: "because he **deems himself** to be free of need." Our translation: "once they **think** they are self-sufficient." Every one of them keeps a verb of perceiving rather than a verb of fact — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the conclusion outright a verse later: **"The proud and arrogant man is thus not self-sufficient."**

So the ayah is not describing a condition. It is describing an illusion, and tracing what the illusion does to a man's behaviour.

**How the illusion works.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the mechanism with beautiful economy: "So long as man is in need of others, he walks straight; but when he thinks that he does not need anyone, he tends towards transgression, and develops the tendency to wrong-doing, tyranny and oppression."

Read that carefully. It is the *felt need* of others that keeps a person walking straight; it is the thought that he needs no one that turns him. The commentary places the pivot exactly there — not in the man's circumstances, but in what he thinks about them.

**Who is at risk.** The commentary refuses to make this only about money. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists: "the affluent people, government officials, and people with abundant children and friends or servants. They become purse-proud and intoxicated with the leadership power they exercise on their groups."

Read that list slowly, because it is wider than most of us assume. Wealth is only the first item. Government office is on the list. A large family and a wide circle of friends and servants are on the list. Ibn Kathir, for his part, ties the state especially to "having an abundance of wealth," and heads this section "The Threat against Man's Transgression for the sake of Wealth." Between the two commentaries, the net is drawn wide: whatever lets a person feel he is free of need is what the ayah is watching.

---

## Ayah 8 — "surely to your Lord is the return"

The cure arrives in a few words. Ibn Kathir introduces it as the moment where "Allah threatens, warns and admonishes him."

**A note on the word.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the word for the return in this ayah, like the word *bushrā*, is a verbal noun — a word that names an action rather than a thing. The meaning the commentary draws from it is sweeping: "all will be returning to their Lord."

**The plain meaning.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: this is "returning to the Lord after death and giving account of good and bad deeds and seeing with their own eyes the evil consequences of arrogance." Note that last phrase — *seeing with their own eyes*. The man of ayah 7 lived by what he could see. He will be answered in the same currency.

Ibn Kathir sharpens the point to the very thing that produced the illusion: "unto Allah is the final destination and return, and He will hold you accountable for your wealth, **as to where you obtained it from and how did you spend it**." Two questions — and neither of them can be answered by a man who imagines the wealth simply belongs to him.

**The deeper meaning.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then opens the ayah out into a sustained argument that no human being has ever been free of need for a single moment, and it is the richest passage in the whole commentary here.

"Though man has been endowed with great natural powers and has been created in the best make, he errs grievously if he thinks that he can ignore Allah's help and guidance. He constantly stands in need of Divine assistance, because his capacities and capabilities — either as an individual or in his collective capacity — are at best limited... If he thinks deeply, he will find that he needs Allah for every movement and pause."

*Every movement and pause.* Not the crises — the ordinary motions of an ordinary hour.

Then comes the second layer of the argument: even at the human level, the fantasy collapses. "Thinking that human beings are not in need of one another is also a fallacy. Allah has made man a social being, and as such he cannot satisfy all his needs by himself." The commentary adds that Allah "has made the social system or network such that all human beings need one another to satisfy their needs some time or the other."

And then the illustration, which is the heart of it:

> "A fresh morsel of food that goes into our mouth and we swallow it unreflecting, is the result of thousands of human beings and animals who worked hard for a long period of time. It is not possible for anyone to engage so many thousands of human beings in his service."

Consider what that means. The bite you swallowed this morning without a thought stands at the end of the long labour of thousands. And the commentary widens it: "The same applies to clothes and other needs which require the services of thousands of millions of humans and animals to prepare the needful things. None of them is his servant. Even if he hires them at a rate of wages to work for him, it would not be possible for him to pay them their wages or salary."

That is the killing blow to ayah 7's illusion. No one could *purchase* the network that feeds and clothes him. So who arranged it?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers: "the system of preparing all his needs is set into motion by the consummate wisdom of the Creator of the universe. He inspired someone to become a farmer, He cast into another's mind to become a woodcutter or a carpenter, He kindled in someone else's mind to become a blacksmith, He stimulated others to be content with labouring or working for somebody else, He ignited in others the burning desire to be involved in commerce or business, trade or industry. In this way, Allah has set up a bazaar of human needs which no government, nor its legal system or an individual could ever set up."

And the conclusion the commentary draws is precisely ayah 8: "A careful thinking along this line must lead us to the natural corollary that *Surely to your Lord is the Return* — that is, we witness that ultimately all things are under Divine power and wisdom."

So notice what has happened. Ayah 8 works on two levels at once. It is a **warning** — you are going back to Him and you will be questioned. And it is a **correction of fact** — you were never independent of Him for a moment; the very illusion of ayah 7 was a misreading of a world that is, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, wholly "under Divine power and wisdom."

---

## Living it

**Interrogate the feeling of not needing anyone.** Ayah 7 locates the trigger in a *perception*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the turning point at the moment "he thinks that he does not need anyone" — so that thought, not the sin that follows it, is the first thing to notice in yourself.

**Audit the whole list, not just the bank balance.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's list included government officials and those with abundant children, friends and servants alongside the affluent. A person can be financially modest and still, in the commentary's phrase, be "intoxicated with the leadership power" he exercises over his group.

**Let the two questions govern your wealth now.** Ibn Kathir says you will be held accountable for your wealth, "as to where you obtained it from and how did you spend it." Those are not exotic questions. They can be asked of this month's income while it is still in your hands.

**Practise the morsel.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's illustration is not decoration — it is an exercise the commentary itself prescribes: "A careful thinking along this line must lead us to the natural corollary that *Surely to your Lord is the Return*." Take one ordinary thing today — a meal, a shirt — and trace back the thousands of hands and the wisdom that arranged them.

The passage does not end its argument here. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes at the close of ayah 7, the ayat that follow "warn such arrogant people about the evil consequences of their behavior."

passages.title: The man who forbids a servant from praying
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These six ayat narrow from a general address to one particular man, on one particular morning, standing over one particular worshipper and telling him to stop praying. What holds them together is a sustained cross-examination. Allah does not open with a threat; He puts questions. Three times the passage begins a line with the same phrase — *a-ra'ayta*, "Have you seen…?" (ayat 9, 11, 13) — and the questions circle the same outrage from different sides: look at what you are doing; look at who you are doing it to. The passage closes not with a punishment but with a question left hanging in the air: **"Does he not know that Allah sees?"** (ayah 14).

## The scene: the Sacred Mosque, and Abu Jahl

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the setting plainly. When the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to perform the ṣalāh, he prayed at first privately, and later in public in the Sacred Mosque. Abu Jahl stopped him from praying and threatened him: if he prayed and prostrated, he would — Allah forbid — trample on his neck.

Ibn Kathir says the same: these ayat "were revealed about Abu Jahl, may Allah curse him," because he threatened the Prophet ﷺ for performing ṣalāh at the Kaʿbah.

Notice what kind of tyranny this is. Abu Jahl was not disputing a doctrine or losing an argument. He was standing in the open sanctuary of Makkah and forbidding a man to put his forehead on the ground. That is the crime this passage indicts.

**Al-Bukhari recorded** that Ibn ʿAbbas said: Abu Jahl said, "If I see Muhammad praying at the Kaʿbah, I will stomp on his neck." This reached the Prophet ﷺ, who said, *"If he does, he will be seized by the angels."* Ibn Kathir notes that At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i also recorded it in their Books of Tafsir, as did Ibn Jarir.

There is a fuller version, which Ibn Kathir reports from Ahmad, At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Jarir, all from Ibn ʿAbbas, and which At-Tirmidhi graded *Hasan Sahih*: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was praying at the Maqām (the prayer station of Ibrahim) when Abu Jahl bin Hisham passed by and said, "O Muhammad! Haven't I prevented you from this?" — threatening him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ became angry with him and reprimanded him. Abu Jahl then said, "O Muhammad! What can you threaten me with? By Allah, I have the most kinsmen of this valley with me." Ibn ʿAbbas added that if he had called his people, the angels of torment would have seized him at that very instant.

And Ibn Kathir records from Ibn Jarir, from Abu Hurayrah, what happened when Abu Jahl actually tried it. He had asked the people whether Muhammad ﷺ covered his face with dust among them — that is, in prostration — and when they said yes, he swore, "By Al-Lāt and Al-ʿUzzā, if I see him praying like this, I will stomp on his neck, and I will certainly put his face in the dust." Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came and began to pray, and the opportunity was there in front of him. The people were astonished, because Abu Jahl began retreating on his heels and covering himself with his hands. Asked what was wrong, he said: "Verily, between me and him is a ditch of fire, monsters and wings." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"If he had come near me, the angels would have snatched him limb by limb."* Ibn Kathir notes that Imam Ahmad bin Hanbal, Muslim, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Abi Hatim all recorded this hadith; the narrator added that Allah revealed an ayah in connection with it, though he said he did not know whether it belonged to this particular report.

Keep that image beside ayah 14. The man who had the most kinsmen in the valley could not take three steps toward a praying man. He never saw what stopped him — but *Allah sees*.

## Three times: "Have you seen?"

The passage is shaped not as an accusation but as an interrogation, and the shape itself is the argument.

**Ayat 9–10 — "Have you seen the man who prevents a servant when he prays?"** The first question simply holds the act up to the light. Ibn Kathir observes that Allah "firstly admonished him with that which was better" — the reasoning comes before the warning. That order is itself a mercy built into the method of the Qur'an.

**Ayat 11–12 — "What if this servant is rightly guided, or encourages righteousness?"** The second question asks Abu Jahl to consider his victim. Ibn Kathir unfolds the two halves precisely: *"Have you seen if he is on the guidance"* means — do you think this man whom you are preventing is upon the straight path **in his action**; *"or enjoins taqwā"* — that is, in his **statements**. Between the two, the whole man is covered: what he does and what he says. And the conclusion is left for Abu Jahl to draw himself. Ibn Kathir puts it as: "Yet, you rebuke him and threaten him due to his prayer."

*Taqwā* — rendered in the translation above as "righteousness" — is the awareness of Allah that makes a person careful, the guard a servant keeps between himself and what would displease his Lord. So the charge is this: the man you are threatening may well be upon the straight path and calling others to be careful of their Lord — and *that* is what you are trying to stop.

**Ayah 13 — "What if that man persists in denial and turns away?"** Here it is worth being honest about the limits of what is in front of us. The commentary we have does not pause on this ayah at all: Ibn Kathir moves directly from *"or enjoins taqwā"* to *"Knows he not that Allah sees."* So the third question is best left to say exactly what it says — denial, and turning away — without a gloss supplied from elsewhere. Where the commentators are silent, it is better to read the ayah and move on than to fill the silence.

## "A servant, when he prays"

There is a quiet dignity in how the worshipper is named in ayah 10. He is not called "Muhammad," nor "the Messenger." He is called *ʿabdan* — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "a slave of Allah," Ibn Kathir "a servant." The Prophet ﷺ is identified here by the title of his servitude, and identified precisely at the moment he is exercising it: *when he prays*.

Two things follow, taking the ayah's own wording as our guide. First, the offence is measured by whose servant is being obstructed: to interfere with a servant is to reckon with his Master. Second, because the wording is *a servant* rather than a name, the words are not sealed shut around one man in one year — the question they ask can be asked of anyone standing over a person at prayer.

## "Does he not know that Allah sees?"

Ayah 14 is the hinge of the whole passage, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out something easy to miss. This ayah, it says, is the response to the threat made by Abu Jahl — and the ayah **does not mention whom Allah is watching**. The object is left open. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes that it is therefore "of general application": Allah is watching the pious person who is performing the ṣalāh, and Allah is watching the wretched, miserable person who is obstructing it. The statement simply asserts that Allah is watching everything and everyone.

Both halves are consolation and warning at once. The worshipper is seen — his prayer is not lost in the noise of a hostile city. The obstructor is seen — his boast, his sneer, his raised foot are all on record. Ibn Kathir puts the second half sharply: does this man who is preventing someone following correct guidance not know that Allah sees him and hears his words, and will compensate him in full for what he has done?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a striking observation about the restraint of the wording. The ayah stops at "Allah is watching." It does not go on to specify what will happen at the Resurrection — because the scenes of that Day are, in its words, unimaginable. The silence is doing work that description could not.

## Living it

**When you are the one being prevented.** The pressure on the Prophet ﷺ was not subtle — a man who boasted of having the most kinsmen in the valley swore to put his face in the dirt. What the passage offers is not an escape route and not a counter-threat, but the fact stated in ayah 14: the One you are praying to is watching. And in the report from Abu Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ simply came and began to pray; it was the man with the raised foot who backed away.

**When you have the power to prevent.** Ayat 11–12 are the questions to ask before obstructing anyone's worship, in any form: what if this person is upon guidance? What if what they are urging is taqwā? Whoever makes ṣalāh difficult for someone — a worker, a family member, a guest — should hear the question of ayah 9 addressed to himself.

**When you are riding high.** Abu Jahl's confidence had a specific fuel, and he named it: "By Allah, I have the most kinsmen of this valley with me." That was the arithmetic he trusted. It bought him nothing at the moment he needed it; he retreated on his heels from a man in prayer and could not explain to anyone what he had seen.

**And the plain comfort of ayah 14.** No act of worship is too small or too obscure to be seen, and no act of oppression is too well-connected to be missed. *Does he not know that Allah sees?*

passages.title: The threat of the forelock and the call to prostrate
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is

These five ayat are the closing thunderclap of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq. A man had threatened the Prophet ﷺ for performing ṣalāh at the Kaʿbah. Allah now answers him directly — first with a warning of what will be done to him (ayat 15–16), then with a mocking invitation to summon whatever backing he thinks he has (ayat 17–18), and finally by turning away from him altogether to address the Prophet ﷺ: ignore him, and go lower in prostration (ayah 19).

What holds the passage together is a single confrontation, seen from Allah's side. A man says *I will stop you from praying*. Allah replies: **We will seize him — and you, prostrate all the more.** Every verse here is either the threat against the obstructor or the command to the one obstructed.

## "But no! If he does not desist" (ayah 15)

Ibn Kathir identifies the man. This portion of the sūrah, he says, was revealed about Abū Jahl, may Allah curse him, who had threatened the Prophet ﷺ for performing ṣalāh at the Kaʿbah. That is the scene ayah 15 opens onto.

**كَلَّا (kallā), "But no!"** — the word that opens the ayah is a word of rejection and rebuke. Ibn Kathir describes what follows as coming "by way of warning and threatening." And the conditional is left deliberately open: *if he does not desist* — if, as Ibn Kathir puts it, he does not recant from his discord and obstinacy. The door is not yet shut. But the consequence named on the other side of that door is severe.

### The forelock

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the Arabic. **لَنَسْفَعًا (la-nasfaʿan)** comes from an infinitive meaning *to seize and drag*. **النَّاصِيَة (an-nāṣiyah)** means the **forelock** — the front part of a person's hair that falls forward over the forehead. And then the observation that makes the image land: *when a person's forelock is seized, he becomes helpless in the hands of the seizer.*

Feel what that picture does. Not seized by the arm, not by the shoulder — by the hair at the very front of the head. It is the grip you use on someone who is finished: no leverage, no dignity, no way to turn the head away. The man who was about to boast of how many kinsmen he could summon is reduced to a creature being dragged by the hair.

Ibn Kathir renders the same phrase differently — "We will scorch his forehead" — and explains: *indeed We will make it extremely black on the Day of Judgement.* So the two commentaries before us hold two readings of what is threatened: the seizing and dragging by the forelock (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān), and the blackening of that forehead on the Day of Judgement (Ibn Kathir). Both attach the punishment to the same spot on the body — the front of the head that a proud man carries high, and that a worshipper puts on the ground.

## A lying, sinful forelock (ayah 16)

Ayah 16 names the forelock rather than the man: *a lying, sinful forelock.* Ibn Kathir explains it directly — the forehead of Abū Jahl is **lying in its statements and sinful in its actions**.

Two words, and between them a whole life is indicted: what this man says, and what this man does. Both corrupted. And the Qur'an fastens both charges onto the forelock itself, as though the part being seized has become the person — the boasting is written on the front of his head, and that is exactly where the grip closes.

## "Let him call his associates" (ayat 17–18)

Ayah 17 is not permission; it is challenge. Ibn Kathir explains **نَادِيَه (nādiyah)** as *his council* — meaning **his people and his tribe**: in other words, let him call them in order to seek help from them.

Ayah 18 answers the summons with a summons. **الزَّبَانِيَة (az-Zabāniyah)**, Ibn Kathir says, are **the angels of torment**. And he gives the purpose in one devastating line: *this is so that he may know who will win — Our group or his group.*

Sit with the mismatch. A man counts heads in a valley. Allah says: call them all; We will call Ours. The whole logic of worldly power — numbers, clan, standing in the assembly — is invited into the arena precisely so that it can be seen to be nothing.

### The narrations behind the threat

Al-Bukhārī recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said: Abū Jahl said, "If I see Muhammad praying at the Kaʿbah, I will stomp on his neck." This reached the Prophet ﷺ, who said: **"If he does, he will be seized by the angels."** Ibn Kathir notes this hadith was also recorded by At-Tirmidhī and An-Nasāʾī in their books of Tafsir, and by Ibn Jarīr.

Ibn Kathir then gives a fuller version, recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās by Ahmad, At-Tirmidhī, An-Nasāʾī and Ibn Jarīr: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was praying at the Maqām (the prayer station of Ibrāhīm) when Abū Jahl bin Hishām passed by and said, "O Muhammad! Haven't I prevented you from this?" — threatening him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ became angry with him and reprimanded him. Abū Jahl answered: "O Muhammad! What can you threaten me with? By Allah, I have the most kinsmen of this valley with me." **Then Allah revealed ayat 17–18** — "Then let him call upon his council. We will call out the guards of Hell!" Ibn ʿAbbās commented: if he had called his people, the angels of torment would have seized him at that very instant. At-Tirmidhī said, "Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ."

That exchange is the hinge of the passage. Abū Jahl's boast was a headcount — *I have more men in this valley than you do.* Ayat 17–18 accept the terms of his challenge and then obliterate them. And note that it was never a live contest at all: on Ibn ʿAbbās's reading, the summons he was invited to make would have finished him on the spot.

Ibn Kathir also relates that Ibn Jarīr recorded from Abū Hurayrah that Abū Jahl asked, "Does Muhammad cover his face with dust while he is among you all?" They said yes. He swore by al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā that if he saw him praying like that he would stomp on his neck and put his face in the dust. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came and began praying, and Abū Jahl had his chance — but the people were surprised to see him retreating backwards on his heels, covering himself with his hands. Asked what was the matter, he said: "Verily, between me and him is a ditch of fire, monsters and wings." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"If he had come near me, the angels would have snatched him limb by limb."** Ibn Kathir notes that Imam Ahmad bin Ḥanbal, Muslim, An-Nasāʾī and Ibn Abī Ḥātim all recorded this hadith.

So the threat of ayat 15–18 was not abstract. The man who swore he would grind that forehead into the dust was himself driven backwards by something he could not see.

**And note where the irony sits.** Abū Jahl's grievance, in that narration, was precisely that Muhammad ﷺ "covers his face with dust." He could not bear the sight of a face lowered to the earth. And the answer of ayah 15 is aimed at his own forelock.

For anyone who has ever felt outnumbered for holding to their prayer, ayat 17–18 are the verses. The count that matters was never the one you can see.

## "Do not obey him — prostrate and draw near" (ayah 19)

Ayah 19 opens with **كَلَّا** again — a second rejection — and then the address changes entirely. Allah stops speaking about the aggressor and starts speaking to His Messenger ﷺ.

Ibn Kathir paraphrases the command: `O Muhammad! Do not obey him in what he is forbidding you from, such as steadfastness in worship and performing worship in abundance. **Pray wherever you wish and do not worry about him.** For indeed Allah will protect you and help you, and He will defend you against the people.` Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same in short: the Prophet ﷺ is advised to ignore and disobey Abū Jahl when he stops him from praying, and to be steadfast in prayer and prostration.

Notice the shape of the response. The threat was aimed at the prayer; the reply is *more* prayer. The command is not "argue with him," not "avoid the Kaʿbah," not even "defend yourself" — Allah reserves the defending for Himself. What is asked is to go down.

**وَاسْجُدْ وَاقْتَرِب — "Fall prostrate and draw near."** The two verbs are joined, and the order is the point: the way up is down. The one position in which a human being is lowest to the ground is the position in which he is nearest to his Lord.

### From the Sunnah: the nearest a servant ever is

Ibn Kathir cites this as confirmed **in the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim**, on the authority of Abū Ṣāliḥ who reported from Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> **"The closest that a servant can be to his Lord is when he is in prostration. Therefore, make abundant supplications."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same hadith from Sayyidnā Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) as being in **Abū Dāwūd**, and adds another authentic Tradition — without naming its collection — with the wording: *because it is fitting and proper that supplications be accepted in the state of prostration.*

This is the answer the sūrah gives to a man who tried to stop a prostration. The very act he was trying to prevent is the act in which a servant stands nearest to Allah — and the moment in which asking is most fitting to be answered.

### Two rulings from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān

**1. Supplicating in sajdah.** It is valid to supplicate while prostrating in the supererogatory (*nafl*) prayer — the voluntary prayers, as opposed to the obligatory ones. In certain narrations, special words of supplication are recorded from the Prophet ﷺ, and it is better to recite those transmitted prayers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that there is no proof or evidence for such supplications in the prostration of the obligatory prayer, because the obligatory prayer needs to be short.

**2. The prostration of recitation.** A prostration is compulsory for the one who recites this verse and for the one who listens to it. A narration of Sayyidnā Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) states that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to prostrate when he recited this verse. Ibn Kathir likewise mentions that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to prostrate at *"When the heaven is split asunder"* (84:1) and at *"Read! In the Name of your Lord Who has created"* (96:1).

So the sūrah does not merely end with a command to prostrate — it makes the reader do it. You reach the last word, *waqtarib*, "and draw near," and then you put your forehead on the ground. The instruction and the obedience are separated by nothing.

## Living it

The passage leaves a believer with a few very concrete things.

**When someone tries to shame you out of your worship, worship more.** That is literally the instruction of ayah 19. Not confrontation, not withdrawal — increase. And with it, the promise Ibn Kathir draws out: *pray wherever you wish and do not worry about him*, because Allah will protect you and help you and defend you against the people.

**Do not be impressed by a crowd.** Ayat 17–18 exist to teach that the side with the numbers is not the side that wins. The Zabāniyah are named specifically so the boaster can learn "who will win — Our group or his group."

**Use your sajdah.** If prostration is the nearest a servant ever comes to his Lord, then the seconds you spend down there are the most valuable seconds you have — and the Prophet ﷺ did not merely inform us of that, he attached an instruction to it: *so make abundant supplications.* In your voluntary prayers, ask there. Prefer the words transmitted from him ﷺ.

**And remember which part of you goes down.** The sūrah threatens a forelock that lied and sinned, and commands a forehead to touch the earth. It is the same piece of a human being. What it does with the ground decides everything.

Ibn Kathir closes his commentary on this sūrah with the words: *Unto Allah is due all praise and thanks, and He is the Giver of success and protection against error.*
